question: Did the risk of a motorist being killed per mile driven in NYC decline from 2013 to 2025? Make a chart and answer based on this crash data.

options.metric: Annual number of motorists killed in police-reported NYC crashes
options.reason: Annual deaths are a direct and easily interpreted measure of the fatal burden recorded in this dataset.
options.answer: The recorded annual count of motorists killed declined from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025 (26.4% lower), but this does not establish a decline per mile driven.
options.interpretation: Because this file has no miles-driven exposure, it cannot establish whether deaths per mile declined; the chart shows the annual number of motorists killed falling from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025. Annual fatalities are a directly observed burden measure, but they leave exposure-adjusted risk per mile unanswered.

options.denominator: Number of police-reported crash records in that calendar year
options.reason: Normalizing deaths by crash-record volume provides a useful comparison when annual crash counts differ.
options.answer: Motorist deaths per 1,000 reported crashes rose from 0.54 in 2013 to 0.95 in 2025 (75.4% higher), so this crash-normalized proxy did not decline, though it is not risk per mile.
options.interpretation: This data lacks miles driven, so it cannot answer whether motorist deaths per mile declined; instead, deaths per 1,000 reported crashes rose from 0.54 in 2013 to 0.95 in 2025. Dividing by crash records provides a crash-volume-adjusted comparison, but it does not measure mileage exposure or individual motorist risk.

answer:
Annual recorded motorist deaths fell from 110 in 2013 to 81 in 2025 (26.4% lower), but this data cannot establish whether risk per mile declined because it contains no miles-driven exposure.
Motorist deaths per 1,000 reported crashes rose from 0.54 in 2013 to 0.95 in 2025 (75.4% higher), but this crash-normalized measure does not show whether risk per mile declined.
